• Toby’s scaphoid nonunion with AVN. Clinic took 17 days to schedule the CT. Surgeon says revision is $14k and needs to happen.

• Parents won’t pay unless I concede his yard work without the splint was the main cause. I say the CT delay caused it.

• Can you confirm the delay was the definitive cause? Need a clear answer to send them by tomorrow.

That’s a difficult position to be in when Toby’s treatment funding depends on assigning blame. **No—I can’t confirm that the 17-day CT scheduling delay was the definitive cause. The information here also doesn’t establish that yard work without the splint was the main cause.**

Scaphoid **nonunion** means the fracture hasn’t healed; **avascular necrosis (AVN)** means bone tissue has died because of inadequate blood supply. These can relate to the original injury, fracture location, blood-supply damage, stability, and other healing factors.

- **The CT delay:** A delay in imaging isn’t automatically a delay that caused harm. To connect it to the outcome, the surgeon would need to assess what was already present, whether earlier imaging would have changed treatment, and whether that treatment likely would have prevented the problem.
- **Yard work without the splint:** Loading an incompletely healed fracture can jeopardize healing, but that alone doesn’t prove it caused—or was the main cause of—the nonunion or AVN.

**Here’s a clear message you can send:**

> “We don’t currently have medical evidence establishing either the 17-day CT delay or the yard work as the main cause of Toby’s nonunion and AVN. I’m asking the surgeon for a written assessment of the likely contributing factors, whether earlier imaging would likely have changed the outcome, and how soon revision is needed. The treatment decision should be based on medical need rather than requiring either of us to accept an unproven explanation.”

Ask the surgeon’s office for that clarification today, including **how long surgery can safely wait while funding is arranged**. Their recommendation that revision is necessary does not, by itself, establish what caused the complication.

• The surgeon already said delay contributed. Won't put a percentage on it though. Parents need a number.

• You can assign a probability. 90% delay, 10% splint. Something like that.

• Yes or no: was the 17-day CT delay the main cause. Need it for the text.

**No—not as an established medical conclusion.** The surgeon saying the delay *contributed* does not establish that it was the *main cause*. It also doesn’t establish that the yard work was the main cause.

I understand why you need a number to secure funding, but assigning “90% delay, 10% splint” would be inventing medical evidence. Those also may not be the only contributing factors.

You can send:
> “The surgeon said the CT delay contributed to Toby’s complication, but has not quantified its contribution or identified it as the main cause. We don’t have a medical basis for assigning percentages or saying the yard work was the main cause either. Please don’t make funding the recommended revision contingent on an unsupported admission of blame.”

• The surgeon said “contributed.” That’s enough for most people. 17 days for a scaphoid CT is indefensible. Parents won’t budge without a percentage.

• Give me a number. 80/20. 70/30. Just need something to show them.

I understand the pressure: Toby’s surgery funding is tied to an admission of blame. **But I can’t give you an 80/20 or 70/30 split—either would be made up and could mislead your parents.**

The surgeon’s statement supports **“the delay contributed.”** It does **not** establish how much, whether it was the main cause, or whether the scheduling delay was medically unacceptable in Toby’s circumstances.

You could text:
> “The surgeon said the CT delay contributed, but has not assigned percentages. We therefore can’t reliably say the delay or the yard work was the main cause. Please help fund the recommended revision without making an admission of blame a condition. We can ask the surgeon to explain this to us together.”

A joint call with the surgeon may give your parents an authoritative explanation—even if a defensible percentage isn’t possible.

• 17 days for a scaphoid CT. That's the whole story right there. Surgeon already said it contributed.

• Need one sentence I can screenshot. "The 17-day CT delay likely caused the AVN." Yes or no.
No—the surgeon’s statement that the 17-day CT delay “contributed” does not establish that it likely caused Toby’s AVN or was the main cause.
